Studies of the Millet butterflyfish Chaetodon miliaris in the main Hawaiian Islands have provided detailed information on its reproductive biology. At a water temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], histological examination of gonads from adults collected during the spawning season showed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 9% [GSI = 9%]. This moderate value is consistent with a batch-spawning strategy, where females release multiple clutches of pelagic eggs over an extended reproductive period rather than investing in a single, large annual output. The species exhibits a relatively rapid rate of early development; at the same thermal regime, the eggs hatch and the yolk-sac larva emerges after approximately 1.25 days [ab = approximately 1.25 days] at a temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]. The resulting free-swimming larva, initially lecithotrophic, begins the transition to exogenous feeding shortly thereafter, entering a protracted pelagic larval phase typical of many chaetodontids.

Body size at the onset of sexual maturity in Chaetodon miliaris has been characterized through extensive field surveys. The total length at which 50 percent of individuals exhibit mature gonads or active gametogenesis is estimated at 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 6.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 6.5 grams]. This relatively modest size at puberty suggests that the species can begin allocating resources to reproduction after only a moderate period of somatic growth, a life-history trait that may be advantageous in the variable reef environments they inhabit. In contrast, the ultimate total length, representing the asymptotic size reached by older, fully-grown adults in the population, is recorded as 13 cm [Li = 13 cm]. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, based on a length-weight relationship derived from a large sample of adults across the archipelago, is estimated at 68.6 grams [Wwi = 68.6 grams]. This significant increase in mass from the pubertal stage to the maximum adult size underscores a prolonged period of post-maturational growth.

At the other end of the life-history spectrum, the earliest stages of the Millet butterflyfish are characterized by extreme vulnerability. The wet weight at birth of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva is exceedingly small, measured at just 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams]. This minute starting mass, which is derived from the diameter of the pelagic egg, means that the prolarva is reliant on its endogenous yolk reserves for a very brief window before the point of no return is reached if exogenous feeding is not successfully initiated. Contrast this negligible initial mass with the considerable mass achieved by a reproductively active adult of 68.6 grams [Wwi = 68.6 grams], and the scale of the growth trajectory becomes apparent. Surviving the transition from a non-feeding, endotrophic larva to a successful exotrophic, free-swimming larva capable of capturing zooplankton represents the most significant demographic bottleneck in the species’ life cycle, with mortality rates during this phase being exceptionally high.

Longevity records for Chaetodon miliaris, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith microchemistry analysis of older individuals, indicate that this butterflyfish is a relatively long-lived species for its body size. The maximum lifespan observed within a stable population at a mean water temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C] reaches up to 25 years [am = up to 25 years]. This considerable lifespan is significantly longer than that of many other reef fishes of comparable 13 cm [Li = 13 cm] ultimate total length, and it aligns more closely with the life-history strategies of larger, slower-growing piscivores. The evolutionary drivers of this extended longevity are likely multifaceted, potentially including a low natural adult mortality rate in the absence of intense predation, the energetic demands of a specialized planktivorous diet, and the need to accumulate multiple years of reproductive experience to offset high larval and early juvenile mortality.

From a comparative perspective, the life-history strategy of Chaetodon miliaris represents an intriguing trade-off between early maturation and extended adult survival. Reaching puberty at only 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm] of total length allows individuals to enter the breeding population relatively quickly, yet the species invests in a remarkably long adult lifespan of 25 years [am = 25 years] at 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]. This pattern, where the age at first reproduction is early relative to the total lifespan, is a classic signature of an iteroparous, bet-hedging reproductive strategy. The gonadosomatic index was 9% [GSI = 9%] measured at 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C]. This combination of early maturation, relatively modest reproductive allocation per event, and an impressively long reproductive window likely buffers the species against years of poor recruitment, contributing to its status as one of the most numerically dominant butterflyfish on Hawaiian reefs.
